papers.title: Same pipelines, different answers: how evaluation design shapes EEG seizure prediction
papers.abstract: Seizure-prediction studies on scalp electroencephalography (EEG) often report accuracies that would be clinically useful, yet the score a model receives also depends on how its test data were separated from its training data. We kept five published pipelines fixed, from a spectral baseline (power spectral density with linear discriminant analysis, PSD+LDA) to a transformer, and changed only how they were evaluated on the CHB-MIT database. When whole subjects were held out in 20 repeated partitions, every pipeline scored close to the 0.5 reference (mean area under the ROC curve, AUC, 0.527-0.553), and the five pipelines differed less from one another than each varied between partitions. Within patients, PSD+LDA reached an AUC of 0.815 when windows were allocated at random but 0.572 when each preictal block was kept intact and later seizures were held out for testing. Tracing every window back to its recording showed that an index-based within-patient split had let raw EEG samples cross the train-test boundary in all ten eligible cases. Thresholds tuned to allow 1.67% false positives on validation data did not hold that rate on new subjects, and at those thresholds only 2-6% of preictal windows were detected. A zero-shot test of the baseline on the Siena database gave an AUC of 0.480. In this benchmark, the choice of evaluation changed the answer far more than the choice of architecture. We release the window manifests, partitions and predictions so that new models can be tested on the same terms. All results concern retrospective window classification, not continuous alarms.

papers.title: A synchronized dual-scale platform combining flexible micro-ECoG and skull-screw EEG reveals frequency-dependent cortex-to-skull spectral gain in awake mice.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is the most scalable window onto brain dynamics, yet how cortical activity is transformed before reaching extracranial electrodes has largely been inferred from forward models rather than directly measured. We built a dual-scale sensing platform in awake mice that records a 16-channel flexible micro-electrocorticography (micro-ECoG) array and five skull-screw EEG electrodes on a single 30-kHz clock, enabling sample-aligned comparison of cortical and skull-level signals. Across 115 simultaneously recorded ECoG-EEG pairs from three mice, cortex-to-skull spectral gain was not frequency-flat but increased with frequency following a power law, indicating that skull EEG relatively preserves high-frequency cortical activity rather than acting as a simple low-pass copy. This gain was also non-stationary: it shifted across blocks of a fixed-order auditory protocol and was not explained by measured video motion, whereas trial-matched cross-scale coherence depended on the reference transform. With channel number equalized, micro-ECoG retained a larger unique spatial component than skull EEG. These results convert the cortex-to-skull relationship from a static modeling assumption into a measurable, frequency- and state-dependent quantity. For neural sensing, they provide an empirical calibration target for choosing electrode scale, reference, and analysis band and for validating EEG forward models and EEG-to-intracranial translation. More broadly, they indicate that noninvasive biomarkers and brain-computer interface features, particularly in high-frequency bands, should be interpreted through frequency- and state-aware cortex-to-skull mappings.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Slow Wave Sleep Detection from Single-Lead EEG in Pediatric Congenital Heart Disease Recovery.
papers.abstract: Slow wave sleep (SWS) is vital for neural recovery and cardiovascular stability in children following congenital heart disease (CHD) surgery. However, pediatric CHD sleep patterns are often disrupted by clinical stressors and exhibit substantial domain discrepancies relative to adult data distributions. To address these challenges, this study establishes the Pediatric Cardiac Post-surgical Sleep (PCPS) dataset, a self-collected and expert-annotated pediatric polysomnography (PSG) dataset specifically targeting the early post-CHD surgical period. We further propose PCPS-SleepNet, an end-to-end deep learning framework for cross-domain sleep staging from single-lead EEG, enabling effective knowledge transfer from public sleep data to pediatric post-surgical CHD data. The architecture employs a multi-band input representation across six sub-bands and leverages a Four-Stage Progressive Encoder integrating Multi-Scale Depthwise Convolution (MSDC) for local features, self-attention for global density modeling, and a Conformer block for hybrid refinement. To mitigate limited pediatric data availability and domain shift, this network is pre-trained on public datasets and fine-tuned on the PCPS dataset. Subject-independent validation showed competitive performance, with an overall accuracy of 75.65 ± 0.58%, an AUROC of 89.06 ± 0.18%, an AUPRC of 83.49 ± 0.13%, and a macro F1-score of 76.68 ± 0.70%. For SWS detection, the model achieved an AUPRC of 87.89 ± 0.20% and an F1-score of 81.55 ± 0.74%. Architectural ablations and frequency-band input contribution analysis supported the model design and suggested the complementary discriminative value of slow-wave frequency-band inputs. These results suggest a practical and patient-friendly sleep detection solution for individualized sleep assessment and rehabilitation in vulnerable pediatric populations.

papers.title: Coordinated Drift of Image Representations in Human EEG
papers.abstract: Sensory representations drift over time in many animal systems, but evidence in humans remains limited. Moreover, how perception remains stable despite representational drift remains unclear. Here, we used THINGS-EEG2, a dataset with multiple sessions of repeated presentations of natural images, to test whether image-evoked EEG responses drift across recording sessions and whether this drift is geometrically constrained. We found that image-specific EEG response patterns drifted in a manner that was coordinated across channels and concentrated along dimensions that encoded image identity. Although this impaired cross-session decoding accuracy on average, its effects were heterogeneous with some image pairs becoming harder to distinguish and others becoming more separable. Critically, global distance statistics and the dimensionality of the image response space were preserved across sessions. Simulations show that downstream Hebbian networks can adapt faster to structured drift that preserves dimensionality than when drift is unstructured. These findings suggest that human sensory representations can change over time while remaining amenable to rapid compensation via unsupervised learning mechanisms.

Simulations indicate Hebbian downstream networks adapt faster to such structured drift than to unstructured drift.

papers.title: Learning discriminative time-frequency representations for EEG segment-level seizure-state classification with channel selection.
papers.abstract: AbstractElectroencephalography (EEG)-based seizure monitoring supports the diagnosis andmanagement of epilepsy; however, high-dimensional multichannel EEG recordings imposesubstantial computational burden and limit suitability for portable monitoring systems.This paper proposes a reduced-channel framework for segment-level classification of EEGinto ictal, preictal and interictal states. It integrates attention-guided EEG channelselection, high-resolution time-frequency analysis via the Time ReassignedMultiSynchroSqueezing Transform (TMSST) and Concentration of Frequency and Time(ConceFT), and a hybrid CNN-BiLSTM classifier. The framework is evaluated on theCHB-MIT and Siena Scalp EEG databases under two complementary protocols: astratified 70/30 holdout split and rigorous Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validationto assess subject independent generalization. Under holdout evaluation using a single EEGchannel, the proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 99.28 ± 0.63%, sensitivity of99.18%, specificity of 99.64%, and MCC of 0.97 on CHB-MIT, and an accuracy of98.75 ± 0.74%, sensitivity of 98.77%, specificity of 99.38%, and MCC(Matthews correlationcoefficients) of 0.97 on Siena. LOSO cross-validation demonstrates subject independentgeneralization, exceeding 91% accuracy on both databases. These results demonstrate thatthe framework achieves an effective balance among segment-level classification accuracy,computational efficiency and reduced-channel operation. Moreover, applicability forportable and wearable EEG-based seizure-state monitoring applications is investigated.

ai.reason: Time-reassigned synchrosqueezing/ConceFT features plus channel selection for segment-level state classification are transferable to sleep/vigilance staging, though the CNN-BiLSTM classifier adds GPU-dependent complexity.
ai.summary: The authors proposed a reduced-channel framework combining attention-guided EEG channel selection, TMSST/ConceFT time-frequency analysis, and a hybrid CNN-BiLSTM classifier for segment-level ictal, preictal, and interictal state classification. With a single EEG channel it reached 99.28% accuracy on CHB-MIT and 98.75% on Siena under holdout evaluation, and exceeded 91% accuracy on both databases under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation.

papers.title: Diphenhydramine disrupts sleep architecture in 5XFAD Alzheimer's disease model and wild-type mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption is common in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diphenhydramine (DPH), a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic properties, is widely used as an over-the-counter sleep aid. We tested whether chronic DPH treatment alters sleep architecture in 5XFAD and wild-type female mice. Female 5XFAD (n = 16) and wild-type (WT) littermates (n = 14) were implanted with wireless telemetry recording devices to measure electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) continuously. After a 24h baseline recording at 5 months of age, mice received oral DPH (10 mg/kg) or vehicle at ZT0 for one month. After this chronic treatment, sleep was recorded continuously for 48h during ongoing dosing. Sleep was scored as rapid eye movement (REM), non-rapid eye movement (NREM) 1, NREM2, or wake. A survival curve analysis was used to investigate the microarchitecture of sleep phases after chronic diphenhydramine treatment. At baseline, 5XFAD female mice had more time in NREM1 than WT female controls and had shorter REM and NREM2 bouts. Chronic DPH treatment fragmented NREM2 in both genotypes, reducing long NREM2 bouts. DPH increased total duration of NREM1 and REM during the active phase, and disrupted the light-dark distribution of sleep. DPH did not rescue 5XFAD sleep deficits; instead, DPH treatment resulted in NREM2 fragmentation. Overall, chronic DPH use degrades sleep quality and increases fragmentation in both WT and AD-model female mice, which questions the use of sedating anticholinergics as sleep aids, especially in AD.

papers.title: Style transfer mapping with ensemble learning for cross-subject EEG-based neuropsychiatric disease recognition.
papers.abstract: Cross-subject electroencephalogram (EEG) recognition remains a fundamental challenge because large inter-subject variability causes severe distribution shifts that substantially degrade the generalization ability of existing learning models. Most existing transfer learning methods attempt to align global feature distributions but often overlook subject-specific structural variations, resulting in unstable adaptation under limited calibration data. To address this problem, we propose a Prototype-Consistent Style Transfer Mapping (PC-STM) framework for cross-subject neuropsychiatric disease recognition. Unlike conventional domain adaptation methods, the proposed framework models subject discrepancy as a prototype-guided style transformation that explicitly aligns target representations with class-consistent source prototypes while preserving discriminative structures. Specifically, a multi-source prototype construction strategy is introduced to characterize representative class distributions, followed by a confidence-aware transductive semi-supervised style transfer module that iteratively refines transformation parameters using labeled calibration samples and unlabeled evaluation samples. Furthermore, a reliability-aware ensemble learning strategy dynamically aggregates multiple subject-specific classifiers according to their calibration consistency, thereby improving robustness against heterogeneous subject distributions. Experiments on two public EEG datasets covering major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease show stable performance under the evaluated leave-one-pair-out protocol. The calibration labels are inherited from the public dataset cohorts or task conditions, and the study does not constitute prospective clinical diagnostic validation. Beyond the evaluated EEG tasks, prototype-guided style transfer may provide a basis for future investigation of other limited-supervision recognition problems.

ai.reason: Prototype-consistent style transfer with small calibration data addresses user calibration and cross-subject generalization, though it targets neuropsychiatric disease rather than sleep.
ai.summary: This paper introduces a Prototype-Consistent Style Transfer Mapping framework with confidence-aware transductive semi-supervised adaptation and reliability-aware ensemble learning for cross-subject EEG-based neuropsychiatric disease recognition, reporting stable performance under a leave-one-pair-out protocol on public EEG datasets of major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: A representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework for spectral analysis and detection of epileptiform patterns in pediatric EEG: computational validation with a roadmap for external benchmarking.
papers.abstract: Pediatric EEG analysis for epilepsy detection is challenged by the non-stationary and developmentally heterogeneous nature of epileptiform activity. Conventional Fourier approaches provide limited time-frequency localization, whereas single-domain methods such as the wavelet transform and empirical mode decomposition (EMD) each exhibit complementary weaknesses. We developed a representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework that integrates wavelet and EMD spectra before feature extraction. The pipeline included adaptive wavelet denoising, energy-criterion EMD, weighted time-frequency fusion, extraction of eight spectral-temporal features, and classification using a soft-voting ensemble of a radial basis function support vector machine, random forest, and neural network. Evaluation was performed on 2,000 synthetic pediatric EEG segments spanning canonical epileptiform morphologies and multiple signal-to-noise ratios. A feature-level fusion variant was implemented as an ablation comparator to isolate the effect of fusion strategy while preserving identical feature extraction, classifier architecture, and validation procedures. Across 10-fold stratified cross-validation with 100 Monte Carlo replications, the proposed framework achieved 94.6 ± 0.6% accuracy, 93.7 ± 0.8% sensitivity, 95.5 ± 0.5% specificity, F1 score of 0.943 ± 0.007, and AUROC of 0.971 (95% CI, 0.962-0.978). Performance exceeded standalone wavelet, EMD, and Fourier baselines (all p < 0.001). Representation-level fusion also outperformed feature-level fusion by 1.4 percentage points in accuracy, with the greatest gains observed for polyspike and slow-wave morphologies. On the synthetic corpus the framework was competitive with EEGNet and a 1D convolutional network while retaining explicit time-frequency interpretability. In an external feasibility validation on the CHB-MIT pediatric scalp EEG corpus (14 subjects, leave-one-subject-out), representation-level fusion attained the highest performance of all methods (AUROC 0.901, accuracy 86.7%), confirming that the fusion strategy transfers to real recordings, with performance decreasing as expected. Representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion provides an interpretable and transparent computational framework for analyzing non-stationary pediatric epileptiform EEG whose advantage over classical time-frequency baselines persists, at feasibility scale, on real CHB-MIT recordings and remains competitive with deep-learning baselines. Because the primary evaluation is synthetic and the external validation is a feasibility-scale demonstration, these figures should be read as evidence of methodological viability and external transportability rather than definitive clinical performance; validation on larger, multi-center and prospective pediatric cohorts is the essential next step.

papers.title: A generative framework for estimating brain energy landscapes from continuous neuroimaging observations.
papers.abstract: Pairwise maximum entropy models (pMEMs) are gaining increasing attention as a principled way to study nonlinear brain-state transitions. By representing each brain region as a binary active/inactive state and estimating the least-biased probability distribution over all such network configurations, pMEMs reconstruct an energy landscape in which local minima correspond to stable or metastable brain states and transitions reflect movement across attractor basins. However, neuroimaging recordings are continuous and spatially mixed, forcing conventional pMEM analyses to demean and hard-threshold each channel. This ad hoc binarization discards amplitude information and can conflate spatially correlated noise or source mixing with genuine neural coupling. We introduce a hierarchical generative pMEM that links latent binary network states to continuous observations. Node-specific baseline and gain parameters model amplitude modulation, compound-symmetry noise captures shared residual covariance, and, for electroencephalography/magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG), the electromagnetic leadfield is included as a generative forward model rather than a preprocessing inverse. Model parameters and latent states are jointly estimated using exact posterior enumeration for the small networks analyzed here and a mean-field extension for larger networks. Controlled simulations demonstrated two complementary advantages of the proposed framework. Residual-covariance modeling improved recovery of pMEM fields, couplings, and latent states by accounting for shared fluctuations, with the clearest gains when residual spatial correlation was sufficiently strong. The generative leadfield model further improved sensor-space inference by avoiding inverse-first source reconstruction, including settings in which covariance modeling alone offered limited gains. Resting-state EEG validation showed higher residual correlation during eyes-closed than eyes-open rest, consistent with elevated and spatially coherent alpha activity. Applied further to propofol sedation EEG (alpha-band amplitude envelopes, 8-13 Hz), the fitted 6-node default mode network (DMN) model showed pipeline-dependent condition effects in residual spatial correlation and basin entropy, not apparent under the conventional demean-based pMEM.

ai.reason: Provides a principled continuous-observation state-space/energy-landscape framework with an EEG/MEG leadfield forward model, matching state-space and dynamical-model interests and adaptable to neural time-series.
ai.summary: The authors introduce a hierarchical generative pairwise maximum entropy model linking latent binary brain states to continuous observations, with node-specific baseline/gain parameters, compound-symmetry noise, and an EEG/MEG leadfield forward model instead of an inverse-first reconstruction. Simulations showed improved recovery of fields, couplings, and latent states, and application to propofol sedation EEG revealed pipeline-dependent condition effects in residual spatial correlation and basin entropy not seen with conventional demean-based pMEM.

papers.title: Detection of Spreading Depolarization with Noninvasive Electroencephalography
papers.abstract: Background and Purpose: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are waves of near-complete breakdown of the transmembrane ion gradients that underlie migraine aura and occur in patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic, ischemic or hemorrhagic brain injury. SDs are involved in primary and secondary brain injury. They are associated with poor neurological outcome and represent a modifiable therapeutic target. However, despite decades of investigation, SD detection still requires invasive subdural electrocorticography (ECoG) using an implanted subdural electrode strip, restricting monitoring to a small subset of neurosurgical patients. Methods: We developed WAVEFRONT, a noninvasive scalp electroencephalography (EEG) biomarker of SD based on spatiotemporal propagation characteristics of delta-band EEG activity. The biomarker was trained and validated using concurrent, multi-day scalp EEG and invasive subdural electrocorticography recordings from patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or malignant hemispheric stroke (MHS) across three institutions. We assessed out-of-sample performance across institutions, diagnosis, and surgical approaches, as well as calibration, temporal synchrony, and spatial specificity relative to gold-standard SDs annotated on ECoG. Clinical utility was further evaluated in 607 patients comatose after cardiac arrest from the multicenter International Cardiac Arrest REsearch (I-CARE) consortium, a population in whom invasive monitoring is not performed. Outcome analyses excluded patients who died (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 5) because death may reflect decisions to withdraw life-sustaining treatment in addition to neurological injury. Results: A total of 1,119 gold-standard SDs were annotated in 32 patients (TBI, n=17; SAH, n=12; MHS, n=3; range 0-187 SDs per patient). Across exhaustive cross-validation and institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, WAVEFRONT models trained on one set of patients consistently maintained high performance when evaluated in previously unseen out-of-group cohorts. At the optimal operating point, WAVEFRONT achieved a mean cross-validated true positive rate of 97.3+/-1% with a false positive rate of 6.0+/-0.5%, calculated over 2-min sliding windows with 30-s overlaps. The cumulative duration of WAVEFRONT detections within 30-hour windows strongly correlated with the number of SDs measured by invasive ECoG (R^2=0.7411). Scalp-detected depressions were spatially consistent with the location of the invasive recording strip, and visual inspection demonstrated close temporal correspondence with invasive detections, including during SD clusters. External validation in the independent I-CARE cohort using WAVEFRONT trained on the invasive-monitoring cohort demonstrated significantly greater SD burden on day 3 of post-arrest EEG monitoring among patients with poor neurological outcome (CPC 3-4, n=29) than those with good outcome (CPC 1-2, n=225; p=0.007). Conclusions: Eight decades after Leao's description of SD in 1944, we propose and validate a noninvasive scalp EEG biomarker of SD. Consistent performance across institution-, diagnosis-, and surgical approach-based hold-out analyses, together with burden calibration, spatial specificity, and temporal synchrony with ECoG detections, supports the validity of the WAVEFRONT framework. The association of biomarker burden with neurologic outcome after cardiac arrest suggests that noninvasive monitoring may enable investigation of spreading depolarizations in populations where invasive monitoring is not feasible. Future studies should evaluate prospective performance, treatment responsiveness, and disease-specific associations of the SD biomarker with clinical outcome.

papers.title: Post-intervention high-beta synchronization tracks stable-manifold alignment during stick-balancing learning
papers.abstract: Learning to stabilize an unstable object may depend not only on the accuracy of active corrective interventions but also on when to suspend intervention and allow the object's intrinsic dynamics to evolve. We investigated learning-related changes in control dynamics and associated beta-band electroencephalographic (EEG) activity during virtual stick balancing. Ten healthy young adults practiced stabilizing a virtual inverted pendulum with a joystick over two consecutive days; scalp EEG was recorded from seven participants. For each control cycle, control quality was quantified as the distance (dist) between the pendulum state at the end of each active intervention phase and the stable manifold of the control-OFF subsystem. With practice, balance duration increased, dist decreased, and the proportion of time without active intervention increased. Time-frequency responses stratified by control quality showed that post-intervention high-beta event-related synchronization was most prominent in cycles with the smallest dist. Single-cycle linear mixed-effects models further revealed an inverse association between post-intervention high-beta power and dist after accounting for intervention magnitude and movement direction, as well as trial progress where applicable. This relationship was evident in both the initial Control and final Skilled task datasets. These findings indicate that stick-balancing practice improves the ability to terminate active intervention near the stable manifold and suggest that post-intervention high-beta synchronization tracks the quality of the transition from active correction to the intrinsic dynamics of the control-OFF subsystem.

ai.reason: Uses stable-manifold state-space framing and time-frequency EEG analysis during motor learning; conceptually relevant to dynamical modeling, though small-N and task-specific.
ai.summary: Investigated learning-related changes in control dynamics and beta-band EEG during virtual stick balancing over two days in healthy adults. With practice, balance duration increased, distance to the stable manifold decreased, and post-intervention high-beta synchronization was inversely associated with that distance, suggesting it tracks the quality of transition from active correction to intrinsic control-OFF dynamics.

papers.title: GeoMind: Dancing with Geometric Brain Rhythm on Symmetric Positive Definite Manifolds.
papers.abstract: State space model (SSM) is a powerful tool in neuroscience field to characterize the dynamic nature of brain functions by elucidating the mechanism of how brain system transits between brain states and how underlying states give rise to the observed neural activities. Although tremendous efforts have been made to lend the power of deep learning and mathematical insight of SSM in various functional neuroimaging studies, current state-of-the-art methods lack a holistic view of brain state evolution as a self-organized dynamical system where each part of the brain is functionally inter-connected. Since the topological co-activation of functional fluctuations exhibits an intrinsic geometric pattern (symmetric and positive definite, SPD) on the Riemannian manifold, the call for understanding how a selective set of functional connectivities in the brain supports diverse behavior and cognition emerge a new machine learning scenario of manifold-based SSM for largescale functional neuroimages. To that end, we propose a geometric neural network of SSM, coined GeoMind, designed to uncover evolving brain states by tracking the trajectory of functional dynamics on a high-dimensional Riemannian manifold of SPD matrices. GeoMind demonstrates promising results in identifying specific brain states on task-based functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) data, as well as in diseases early diagnosis for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and Autism, by using resting-state fMRI. These results highlight the applicability of GeoMind in neuroscience research. To further evaluate generalizability of GeoMind, we applied GeoMind to electroencephalography (EEG) emotion datasets, outperforming competing methods and demonstrating scalability across neuroimaging modalities.

papers.title: Robust Epilepsy Diagnosis in Neonates Via Spatio-Temporal Graph Learning and Balanced Test-Time Training.
papers.abstract: Timely diagnosis of neonatal epilepsy is critical for mitigating long-term neurodevelopmental deficits. However, while neonates exhibiting extensive seizure burden are readily identified, accurately diagnosing epileptic infants with sparse or no overt seizure onset during monitoring remains a formidable challenge using electroencephalogram (EEG) signals alone. Current automated systems predominantly target ictal-specific seizure detection, limiting their clinical utility for risk stratification during seizure-free intervals (interictal), particularly given the pronounced EEG variability across neonates. This work presents a cross-subject deep learning framework that robustly distinguishes epileptic from "healthy" neonates by integrating dynamic graph topology with self-supervised adaptation. Our architecture models multichannel EEG as spatio-temporal graphs to capture functional connectivity, while a balanced test-time training mechanism dynamically adapts the model to unseen patients via masked signal reconstruction. This effectively mitigates the domain shifts caused by inter-subject variability without requiring patient-specific labels. Validated on a clinically curated cohort of 140 neonates (70 healthy, 70 epileptic), our approach achieves a segment-level accuracy of 83$\%$ and an area under the curve of 0.90. For the primary subject-level endpoint, accuracy increases from 0.79 without adaptation to 0.88 with balanced TTT, using aggregation thresholds selected on inner validation subjects and fixed before evaluation on each held-out fold. The cohort includes anoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, benign neonatal convulsions, and cerebrovascular accident. Analyses restricted to non-ictal windows also support discrimination between the two groups, although all neonates in the epilepsy group experienced seizures elsewhere in their recordings.

ai.summary: Presented a cross-subject deep learning framework for neonatal epilepsy diagnosis from EEG that models multichannel signals as spatio-temporal graphs with balanced test-time training for domain adaptation. On 140 neonates (70 healthy, 70 epileptic) it achieved segment-level accuracy of 83% and AUC 0.90, with subject-level accuracy rising from 0.79 to 0.88 with balanced test-time training.

papers.title: BTBD9-driven IMPDH2 ubiquitination governs sleep homeostasis by gating adenosine metabolism in the basal forebrain.
papers.abstract: BTB domain containing 9 (BTBD9) is among the most reproducible genetic risk factors for sleep-related disorders, yet its molecular function in sleep regulation remains unclear. Here, we aimed to define the downstream substrate, core brain region, and molecular mechanism through which BTBD9 regulates sleep-wake homeostasis. Population-scale genomic and brain expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) datasets were integrated to infer the direction of BTBD9-associated genetic risk in sleep-related traits. Basal forebrain-specific neuronal manipulation of Btbd9 was combined with electroencephalography/electromyography (EEG/EMG)-based sleep analysis and fiberphotomerty to define the relevant brain locus and functional output. Ubiquitinomics, protein interaction, ubiquitination, and enzymatic assays were used to identify BTBD9-regulated substrates and determine how BTBD9-dependent modification affects metabolic enzyme activity. Basal forebrain-specific genetic disruption, receptor pharmacology, and adeno-associated virus (AAV)-delivered interfering peptides were further applied to test pathway necessity and reversibility in vivo. human genetic analyses showed that BTBD9 variants associated with higher expression predicted a pro-arousal tendency. Consistently, neuron-specific deletion of Btbd9 in the mouse basal forebrain increased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and extracellular adenosine levels. Mechanistically, IMPDH2, the rate-limiting enzyme in de novo purine biosynthesis, was identified as a substrate of the Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase 3 (CRL3)BTBD9 ubiquitin ligase. papers.title: Magnetoencephalography in Parkinson's disease: diagnostic potential and barriers to clinical translation.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a heterogeneous neurodegenerative disorder with motor and nonmotor manifestations. Diagnosis remains primarily clinical, and validated markers of early disease and subsequent progression are still needed. Magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures neuronal magnetic fields with millisecond temporal resolution and provides a means of characterizing cortical dysfunction. This narrative review critically synthesizes MEG evidence on periodic and aperiodic spectral activity, functional connectivity, network topology, and individual brain fingerprinting, with emphasis on diagnostic relevance and barriers to clinical translation. Recurring findings include spectral slowing and cognitive-network disruption, whereas resting β power, burst dynamics, and coupling depend on clinical phenotype, treatment state, and analytical choices. Evidence from electroencephalogram (EEG), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and invasive recordings is distinguished from direct MEG findings. Internally validated classification of established PD and healthy controls is promising, but does not establish performance in prodromal disease or clinically uncertain parkinsonism. Optically pumped magnetometers may improve recording flexibility while retaining requirements for environmental interference control. Prospective clinical cohorts, standardized acquisition and analysis, reproducibility studies, independent validation, and comparison with clinical assessment are needed to establish incremental diagnostic and prognostic utility.

papers.title: Beyond Static Representations: Learning Electroencephalogram Spatiotemporal Dynamics for Enhanced Emotion Recognition.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based emotion recognition plays a pivotal role in brain-computer interfaces and mental health monitoring. However, conventional approaches often neglect the intrinsic spatial correlations among EEG channels and fail to effectively model both global temporal dependencies and the continuity of neural oscillations. To overcome these challenges, we propose the Dynamic Spatial Embedding and Temporal Attention Mamba (DSE-TAM) framework. Our Dynamic Spatial Embedding (DSE) module leverages graph convolutional networks to dynamically capture inter-channel relationships, preserving spatial coherence in EEG representations. Subsequently, the Temporal Attention Mamba module integrates self-attention with state-space models to jointly optimize long-range temporal dependencies and smooth transition dynamics. Extensive experiments on 2 public benchmarks (DEAP and DREAMER) and an in-house CEED dataset demonstrate that DSE-TAM surpasses state-of-the-art methods, achieving accuracies of 79.75% (arousal) and 78.27% (valence) on DEAP, 80.55% (arousal) and 83.91% (valence) on DREAMER, and 73.75% (3-class) on CEED. These results validate the framework's efficacy in advancing EEG-based emotion decoding for brain-computer interfaces. The source code is available at https://github.com/Raizeroko/DSE-TAM.

papers.title: Replacing EEG with peripheral physiological signals for driving behavior recognition: a physiology-informed multimodal approach.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) has been widely used for driving behavior recognition due to its ability to capture neural activity; however, EEG acquisition typically requires expensive hardware and complex instrumentation, which limits its practicality in real-world applications. A publicly available multimodal driving dataset collected in a simulator environment was analyzed, containing physiological recordings from 35 participants performing five driving behaviors, including smooth driving, acceleration, deceleration, lane change, and turning. Three peripheral physiological signals-electrocardiography (ECG), electromyography (EMG), and galvanic skin response (GSR)-were integrated using a physiology-informed multimodal learning framework designed to capture complementary physiological responses and temporal dynamics across modalities. Experimental results show that the proposed peripheral multimodal configuration (ECG+EMG+GSR) achieves an average accuracy of 0.795 and macro-F1 score of 0.805 under five-fold cross-validation, with MCC and Cohen's kappa reaching 0.731 and 0.730, respectively. Controlled comparisons with six representative baseline methods further showed that the proposed framework consistently outperformed all competing methods across different physiological modality configurations. Notably, the ECG+EMG+GSR configuration outperformed the EEG-only setting while avoiding EEG acquisition and its associated multi-electrode setup, thereby providing strong recognition performance with substantially lower sensing burden and deployment complexity. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal peripheral physiological sensing as a practical and cost-efficient alternative to EEG for driving behavior recognition in intelligent transportation systems.

Overall, these findings underscore the potential of the TS-DTB to advance the mechanistic understanding of the brain and inform personalized digital therapeutics.

papers.title: Interictal epileptic discharge > 1% associated with cognitive impairment in adult patients with epilepsy: A cross-sectional study based on dose-response relationship and discharge characteristics.
papers.abstract: Epilepsy is frequently accompanied by multidomain cognitive impairment, but the quantitative contribution of interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs)-including discharge burden, vigilance state, and spatial distribution-to specific cognitive domains remains incompletely defined. This cross-sectional study aimed to examine associations between multidimensional IED parameters and domain-specific cognitive function in non-symptomatic adult epilepsy. After adjustment for age, education, disease duration, seizure duration, seizure frequency, and antiepileptic drug count, a sleep IED index > 1% remained associated with lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment, associative learning, and verbal fluency scores versus the < 1% group; Mini-Mental State Examination was borderline and visual recognition did not survive FDR. For wakefulness, no significant graded association emerged between < 1% and > 1% groups; versus no discharge, wake > 1% showed lower Digit Symbol and verbal fluency scores at uncorrected level only. Discharges during both sleep and wakefulness were associated with lower backward digit span than sleep-only discharges, with a trend after FDR. Lateralization and focal/multifocal distribution were not significantly associated after FDR. Frontal IEDs were associated with lower verbal fluency and attention-related scores versus no discharge, but direct regional contrasts were nonsignificant and limited by small subgroups. A sleep IED index > 1% may represent a candidate electrophysiological marker of domain-specific cognitive vulnerability, whereas a wakefulness threshold and clear regional specificity were not definitively established. Furthermore, we characterized the link between changes in E/I and motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) with levodopa administration. We suggest that characterizing individual responses to specific treatments is a fundamental step in tailoring rehabilitation protocols and optimizing intervention efficacy.

papers.title: Computational approaches to deep learning-driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson's disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.

papers.title: Federated Spiking GANs with Rényi Differential Privacy for privacy-preserving synthetic EEG generation in brain-computer interfaces.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data used in brain-computer and brain-machine interfaces (BCI/BMI) contain sensitive, user-specific information, creating privacy risks in consumer applications such as gaming, human augmentation, and virtual reality. No significant interaction effects were found for delta, alpha, or beta power. Conclusions: Sequential motor-cortex rTMS followed by repeated bilateral 10-Hz tACS was associated with increased resting-state theta activity in fibromyalgia. Given the small sample size, post hoc ROI selection, lack of sham stimulation, and absence of component-specific control conditions, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication in adequately powered sham-controlled studies.

papers.title: Applications of functional ultrasound brain-computer interfaces in neurological diseases: research progress based on neurovascular coupling.
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) bypass peripheral nerves and muscles to establish direct information pathways between the brain and external devices, providing novel approaches for motor function reconstruction, communication assistance, and neurorehabilitation in patients with neurological disorders. However, conventional non-invasive BCIs relying on modalities such as electroencephalography (EEG), magnetoencephalography (MEG), or functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) exhibit limitations in spatiotemporal resolution, portability, or real-time capability. Functional ultrasound (fUS), an emerging neuroimaging technology based on neurovascular coupling (NVC), detects cerebral blood volume changes at a spatial resolution of approximately 100 μm; its imaging frame interval is 200-500 ms, whereas its effective temporal resolution, limited by the hemodynamic response, is 1-2 s, offering a potential solution to overcome these constraints. This review comprehensively analyzed NVC-based fUS brain-computer interfaces from the dimensions of technical principles, clinical applications, future directions, and challenges. fUS has demonstrated significant clinical value in stroke assessment, epilepsy monitoring, and early identification of neurodegenerative diseases. Emerging technologies such as transcranial focused ultrasound neuromodulation, sonogenetics, and intravascular ultrasound are driving the evolution of fUS from single-signal "acquisition" toward bidirectional "acquisition-modulation" closed-loop systems, which remain at the proof-of-concept stage. However, the hemodynamic response latency relative to neural electrical activity (1-2 s), the yet-unclear biosafety of chronic ultrasound exposure, and insufficient decoding reliability under pathological conditions remain critical bottlenecks requiring urgent resolution. In conclusion, NVC-based fUS brain-computer interfaces provide a novel tool for precision diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases. Future efforts should focus on conducting multicenter clinical trials and enhancing the robustness of decoding algorithms.

papers.title: Assessment of the duration of continuous EEG monitoring in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can detect seizures and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Because a standard duration of continuous EEG monitoring to capture these complications has not been established in aSAH, we compared a standard 6- or 7-day cEEG monitoring protocol versus longer periods of monitoring. We performed a retrospective analysis of aSAH patients ≥18 years old grouped by standard monitoring protocol (6-7 days, group 1) and those with longer monitoring (>7 days, group 2). Clinical characteristics, EEG features, length of stay (LOS) and functional outcome were compared using univariate analyses. Multivariable analyses tested the association between the groups and vasospasm, DCI, LOS, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS). 19 patients met criteria for group 1 and 16 patients for group 2. We found no difference in EEG's detection of worsening abnormal EEG activity, vasospasm and DCI. ICU and hospital LOS in group 2 were nearly double that of group 1 (ICU: 25.5 (19.5-35) vs. 14 (11-21) days, p = 0.0003; hospital: 32.5 (29.5-48) vs. 18 (13-29) days, p = 0.003). Good outcome (mRS ≤2) at discharge and at 6 months was similar in both groups (21.1% vs. 0% and 56.3% vs. 46.2%). In multivariable analysis, EEG duration was independently associated with ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and mRS at 6 months. Longer EEG monitoring correlated with significantly longer ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and functional outcome at 6 months. Larger studies to confirm our findings are warranted.

papers.title: Impact of burst suppression duration on delirium and its diagnostic value in mechanically ventilated ICU patients.
papers.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium affects up to 50% of mechanically ventilated patients. This condition is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Although bispectral index (BIS) monitoring is widely used for sedation assessment, its predictive value for delirium remains limited. Burst suppression (BS) is an electroencephalographic pattern reflecting profound cerebral dysfunction. BS has been proposed as a predictor of delirium. However, the quantitative role of burst suppression duration (BSD) in delirium risk stratification has not been established. This prospective observational study enrolled 300 mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients between April 2021 and October 2024 at Harrison International Peace Hospital. Continuous video-electroencephalogram (vEEG) monitoring was performed. BSD was quantified from the vEEG recordings. Delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of BSD. Among 300 patients, 130 (43.3%) developed delirium. The delirium group had significantly longer BSD than the control group (median 81.1 s, IQR 41.5-148.5 vs. 17.2 s, IQR 5.8-32.9; P < 0.001). Multivariate analysis identified BSD (adjusted OR = 1.018, 95% CI 1.012-1.023; P < 0.001), BIS (adjusted OR = 0.964, 95% CI 0.946-0.982; P < 0.001), age (adjusted OR = 1.024, 95% CI 1.002-1.047; P = 0.031), and hypertension (adjusted OR = 1.748, 95% CI 1.002-3.051; P = 0.049) as independent risk factors. ROC analysis demonstrated that BSD achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.871 (95% CI 0.829-0.913). The optimal cutoff of 41.5 s yielded a sensitivity of 80.8% and a specificity of 78.2%. The combination of BSD and BIS improved the AUC to 0.914 (95% CI 0.882-0.946). BSD is an independent risk factor for delirium in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. It demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy as a quantitative biomarker. The combination of BSD and BIS provides superior predictive performance. This combined approach offers a practical quantitative tool for early delirium risk stratification.

papers.title: EEG monitoring in the neonate as part of a multimodal brain protection system in paediatric anaesthesia.
papers.abstract: Neurological monitoring is well established in anesthesia. Applied for assessment and control it also provides indirect information on hemodynamic status, ventilation, oxygenation and perfusion. In pediatric anesthesia, the potential toxicity of anesthetics is a concern. In neonates and young infants, the brain is immature and still developing, making electroencephalogram monitoring complex. To determine the current state of neurological function monitoring in neonates during anesthesia as a brain protection tool, a narrative review was conducted. The search prioritized the last ten years in PubMed, Cochrane, other electronic sources, and snowball sampling using the keywords: Neurotoxicity, Brain Monitoring, Newborn, Anesthesia, Neuroprotective Strategies, combinations thereof, and expert publications. The review concludes that brain protection is necessary, however further knowledge and validated technological support are required.

papers.title: Elaborative processing before retrieval practice enhances semantic organization and long-term memory.
papers.abstract: One longstanding goal in psychology is to identify more effective ways of learning. Recent work has shown that elaborative processing can amplify the memory benefits of retrieval practice, yet the mechanisms underlying this advantage remain unclear. Using electroencephalography (EEG), the present study examined how elaborative processing before retrieval practice influences later memory and encoding-related neural processing and representations, relative to context processing. Behaviorally, memory performance was better for elaborative processing plus retrieval practice than for context processing plus retrieval practice. During the first encoding phase, elaborative processing elicited a more negative N400, whereas context processing elicited a more positive LPC. Moreover, the N400 and LPC differences between elaborative and context processing during encoding were significantly correlated with the corresponding differences in 7-day recognition performance. Representational similarity analyses further showed stronger semantic-category organization and greater representational reorganization across repeated encoding under elaborative processing than under context processing. These findings suggest that elaborative processing before retrieval practice enhances long-term memory and is associated with broader semantic processing and stronger semantic organization during encoding. More broadly, the results suggest that richer connections with pre-existing semantic knowledge may be one way in which encoding variability supports long-term memory.

papers.title: Making sense of touch: Spatial tactile cues promote efficient visuo-somatosensory integration and restore motor accuracy under sensory conflict.
papers.abstract: Effective interaction with complex environments relies on the integration of somatosensory and visual signals into coherent spatial representations of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, as during goal-directed hand movements under mirror-reversed visual feedback, motor performance deteriorates. Despite this conflict, the visual mapping between the hand and the environment remains preserved, and visual information typically facilitates motor performance, whereas tactile feedback impairs it. Here, we tested whether providing tactile input with explicit spatial structure renders visuo-somatosensory integration functionally relevant and stabilizes motor behaviour under sensory conflict. Healthy adults performed a mirror-tracing task, tracing a shape's contour with the index finger while tactile feedback conveyed either motion-related cues alone or additional discrete spatial landmarks aligned with the outline. Spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness relative to motion-related tactile input, indicating more effective online motor control. EEG source analyses further revealed that, when spatial tactile cues were present, somatosensory activity increased and functional connectivity was largely restricted to sensorimotor areas. In contrast, when tactile cues did not convey spatial information, sensory conflict was associated with widespread reductions in cortical activity, including in somatosensory and parietal areas, and with a diffuse functional connectivity pattern consistent with elevated sensorimotor uncertainty. Together, these findings indicate that providing spatial structure to tactile input can mitigate the detrimental effects of visuo-somatosensory conflict on motor performance and support more efficient integration of visual and somatosensory information during action. KEY POINTS: Accurate movements depend on combining visual and somatosensory information to estimate the position of the body in external space. When these signals conflict, motor performance usually deteriorates and tactile feedback can become disruptive. We tested whether tactile feedback becomes useful for movement control when it provides explicit spatial landmarks, rather than only motion-related information from finger-surface contact. During a tracing task under visuo-somatosensory conflict, spatially structured tactile cues preserved movement accuracy and smoothness compared with when touch conveyed motion cues alone. Spatial tactile cues were associated with increased somatosensory cortical activity and a more spatially restricted pattern of functional coupling within sensorimotor networks, whereas their absence was associated with reduced somatosensory and parietal activity and a more distributed connectivity profile. Spatial structure in touch promotes multisensory integration, helping stabilize motor control under sensory conflict and highlighting how tactile cue design may improve sensorimotor function.

papers.title: A mechanistic classification of GNAO1 mutations links Gβ γ sequestration to hyperkinetic disease and treatment response
papers.abstract: Go is the most prevalent G protein subunit in the brain and is critical for signal transduction through G protein-coupled receptors. Mutations in the gene encoding Go (GNAO1) cause a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with involuntary movements (NEDIM) and, in some patients, developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Here, we integrate human genetic analysis with cellular assays to define mechanistic classes of GNAO1 mutations and in vivo approaches to evaluate therapeutic strategies. We grouped variants into two functional categories: those predicted to sequester G{beta}{gamma} and those with reduced Go expression and therefore increased G{beta}{gamma} signaling. Analysis of patient data revealed that mutations predicted to impair G{beta}{gamma} release are significantly associated with NEDIM. Using the GNAO1R209H/+ mouse as a model of NEDIM, we evaluated two small molecules: caffeine, a nonselective adenosine receptor antagonist, and gallein, a selective modulator of G{beta}{gamma}-effector interactions. Both compounds significantly reduced hyperlocomotion in the open field test. Whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology revealed sex- and cell type-specific hyperexcitability in spiny projection neurons within the dorsolateral striatum of GNAO1R209H/+ mice. Together, these findings implicate dysfunction of dorsolateral striatal pathways in GNAO1-related disorder and suggest that mechanistic understanding of disease variants can guide targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.
papers.abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.
